## Warm-up – the three Rs {#task-1-concepts-warm-up-while-the-engine-loads}

The warm-up settles the vocabulary before you touch any data. Three of the four scenarios below describe one of our three Rs – reproducibility, robustness, replicability – and the fourth describes something else. Read all four, then label each one in the code cell.

***Scenario 1:*** A reviewer reruns the authors' Stata .do file on the authors' data and gets a *different* coefficient from the one printed in the paper. This is an example of \_\_\_\_\_\_ even though what they *tried* to do failed.

***Scenario 2:*** The analyst uses the authors' submitted replication dataset, but they re-implement the model in R instead of Stata and centre the predictor. Is this a case of  \_\_\_\_\_\_ or \_\_\_\_\_\_?

***Scenario 3:*** A preregistered team tests the identical hypothesis on a *separate, much larger* dataset chosen to be theoretically equivalent, and gets results that contradict the original. Their conclusion is that the original analysis has failed to \_\_\_\_\_\_.

***Scenario 4:*** Instead of the survey data used by the original authors, another researcher tests the same underlying idea on social-media texts using a machine-learning classifier method that the original never used. To their surprise, the authors' original findings turn out to be \_\_\_\_\_\_, and the researcher concludes that they provide a reliable middle-range theory of the phenomenon they investigate.

Fill in the gaps in the code cell below and run it to print your answers back.

```{webr}
#| exercise: vocab
#| code-overflow: wrap

writeLines(c(
  "Scenario 1: This is an example of ______.",
  "Scenario 2: Is this a case of ______ or ______?",
  "Scenario 3: The original analysis has failed to ______.",
  "Scenario 4: The authors' original findings are ______."
))

```

:::: {.solution exercise="vocab"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Answers

1.  **reproducibility** – rerunning the same code on the same data. Here it *failed* to match, but the activity is still reproducibility, and 'not reproduced' is the verdict.
2.  arguably still **reproducibility**, in a grey area – re-implementing on the same data in different software is technically a re-computation – but centring the predictor nudges towards **robustness**. Two packages can also implement the same estimator differently, so make sure you know what the function you call is doing.
3.  **replicability** – same question, independent new data chosen to be theoretically equivalent.
4.  **generalisability** – the odd one out, with new data *and* a new method at once. It is the fourth cell of the matrix, outside the three that the exercise tests.
:::
::::




## Task 2 – Meet the panel {#task-2-get-the-data-and-look-at-it}

The **EU-frames dataset** (`EUframes_cy.csv`) is already loaded for you as `euframes`. It is the country-year panel behind the whole exercise. The copy that this page loads is byte-identical to the one published in the analyst's fork on OSF (osf.io/6zqct – "Multi100 \| Teney_EurSocioRev_2016 \| Analyst_C6HJR", main folder), and the official Multi100 archival record is at osf.io/8rtwe. The downloadable workspace contains the same file.

Run the two cells below to inspect the panel. Edit them freely – this is your environment. The first lists the columns of the panel, with the type and the first values of each.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
datawizard::data_peek(euframes)
```

The second counts the countries, the years and the rows.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
c(countries = insight::n_unique(euframes$cntry), years = insight::n_unique(euframes$year),
  rows = nrow(euframes))
```

You should see **270 rows**, **27 countries**, **10 years** (2004–2013), and 13 columns. The outcome we care about first is `mcosmo`, the mean 'cosmopolitan' framing of the EU in each country-year, on a 0–1 scale. The predictor is `unemp`, the annual unemployment rate. `growth` is annual GDP growth, and `n_cy` is the number of survey respondents in each country-year. The [codebook](data/EUframes_cy_codebook.md) describes the other framings and every remaining column.

Tables print in this lab as plain text, as they would in the console of your IDE. To read one as a formatted table, add `|> gt::gt()` to the end of a cell that prints a data frame and run it again. For the tables of coefficients in Task 3, `|> parameters::print_html()` does the same and also rounds the numbers. In your own IDE and in the report of the workspace, `tinytable::tt()` does this job, but it cannot display its tables on this page.

Now look at the outcome over time, one small panel per country:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
# tinyplot draws on the graphics of base R (McDermott, Arel-Bundock and
# Zeileis, tinyplot, CRAN, doi:10.32614/CRAN.package.tinyplot): the lines
# first, one panel per country, then the points added on top
tinyplot::tinyplot(
  mcosmo ~ year, facet = ~cntry, data = euframes, type = "l", col = "grey55",
  facet.args = list(ncol = 6), xaxb = c(2004, 2008, 2013), theme = "minimal",
  main = "Cosmopolitan EU framing by country, 2004–2013",
  xlab = "", ylab = "Mean cosmopolitan framing"
)
tinyplot::tinyplot_add(type = "p", col = "black", pch = 16, cex = 0.6)
```

In most countries the framing changes little over the decade, while in a few it moves sharply around the 2009 crisis. This variation within a country over time is what the fixed-effects models in Task 3 use.

## Task 2, continued – the estimand and the graph {#task-4-estimand-and-dag}

Before fitting anything, say what you are trying to estimate, in words. A template you can adapt:

> The **unit-specific quantity** is the change in mean cosmopolitan EU framing within a country from one year to another associated with a one-point change in that country's unemployment rate. The **target population** is EU member states over 2004–2013. The **aggregation** is a weighted average of those unit-specific effects, in which the country-years whose unemployment departs most from their country and year means count most, holding fixed each country's time-invariant traits and each year's EU-wide shocks.

That last clause is a causal claim, and a directed acyclic graph (DAG), a diagram in which arrows run from cause to effect, makes it checkable, as the [module on causal graphs](../../companion/dags.qmd#sec-arrows) explains. The graph below draws the five arrows that this exercise takes as given, which the rest of this page calls the committed arrows, and further down you decide which of the arguable arrows to add to them.

```{r}
#| label: dag-reference
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-cap: "The committed graph: unemployment to framing, with country and year each a common cause of both. The three pale nodes have no arrows yet."
ncl_blue <- "#0e3b6a"
orange   <- "#E69F00"
grey_mid <- "#848c94"

dag_ref <- ggdag::dagify(
  framing      ~ unemployment,
  framing      ~ country,
  unemployment ~ country,
  framing      ~ year,
  unemployment ~ year,
  exposure = "unemployment",
  outcome  = "framing",
  coords = list(
    x = c(unemployment = 0, framing = 3, country = 1, year = 2),
    y = c(unemployment = 0, framing = 0, country = 1.4, year = 1.4)))

# dagify() holds edges, so a node with no arrows cannot live in the graph
# object; the three undecided nodes join at the drawing layer instead.
floaters <- tibble::tribble(
  ~name,            ~x,   ~y,
  "growth",         0.9, -1.0,
  "bailout",        1.5, -1.2,
  "politicisation", 3.0, -0.95)

roles <- tibble::tribble(
  ~name,            ~role,       ~disp,
  "unemployment",   "predictor", "unemp.",
  "framing",        "outcome",   "framing",
  "country",        "adjusted",  "country",
  "year",           "adjusted",  "year",
  "growth",         "candidate", "growth",
  "bailout",        "candidate", "bailout",
  "politicisation", "candidate", "politic.")

dag_tidy <- ggdag::tidy_dagitty(dag_ref)
ggdag::update_dag_data(dag_tidy) <- ggdag::pull_dag_data(dag_tidy) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(floaters) |>
  dplyr::left_join(roles, by = "name") |>
  dplyr::mutate(role = factor(role, levels = c("predictor", "outcome", "adjusted", "candidate")))

ggplot2::ggplot(dag_tidy, ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_edges_arc(curvature = 0.18, edge_colour = grey_mid,
                            edge_width = 1.1,
                            arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(9, "pt"),
                                                type = "closed")) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_point(ggplot2::aes(fill = role), shape = 21, size = 26, stroke = 0,
                        colour = "white") +
  ggdag::geom_dag_text(ggplot2::aes(label = disp, colour = role), size = 3.6,
                       fontface = "bold") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c(predictor = orange, outcome = ncl_blue,
                                        adjusted = "#c7ccd2", candidate = "#dde2e7"),
                             guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(predictor = "#FFFFFF", outcome = "#FFFFFF",
                                          adjusted = ncl_blue, candidate = "#5d666e"),
                               guide = "none") +
  ggdag::theme_dag() +
  ggplot2::expand_limits(x = c(-0.5, 3.5), y = c(-1.7, 1.9))
```

Five arrows are drawn. `unemployment -> framing` is the path of interest. Above it, `country` is a common cause of both: stable national traits such as size, EU tenure and labour-market institutions move local unemployment and shape how people frame the EU. `year` does the same job for the EU-wide shocks that hit every country in the same calendar year. The three pale nodes below have no arrows yet, because whether they belong is your decision.

You build the graph yourself in the cells below, in ordinary R. `dagify()` takes one formula per arrow, written the way you write a model, so `framing ~ unemployment` is the arrow that runs *into* `framing`. Read the tilde as 'is caused by' rather than 'is regressed on' and the direction comes out right every time. Because each arrow is its own line of R, an arrow you are unsure about can stay in the cell commented out, and adopting it means deleting a `#`.

`dagify()` and `adjustmentSets()` are already available on this page. In the downloadable workspace they come from `ggdag` and `dagitty`, the R packages for causal graphs, which cannot run here, so `adjustmentSets()` prints the answer that dagitty gave for every combination of the arrows in the cell ([codebook](data/dag_answers_codebook.md)), and any other graph gets a pointer to the workspace.

```{webr}
#| include: false
#| autorun: true
# Graph machinery for Task 2. dagify() reads a graph from one formula per
# arrow, written effect ~ cause as ggdag::dagify() reads it in the workspace.
# adjustmentSets() prints the answer of dagitty from data/dag_answers.csv:
# R/eu-frames/14_dag_answers.R in the course repository computes it with
# dagitty for every combination of the arrows in the graph cell below.
# dagitty itself cannot run on this page, because it reaches its graph
# algorithms through a JavaScript engine that a browser grants only to a page
# served with cross-origin isolation headers (COOP and COEP), and the course
# site does not send them. Any other graph goes to dagitty in the downloadable
# workspace. The table arrives with the page through its `resources:` list.
.dag_answers <- utils::read.csv("data/dag_answers.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE, # r-style: keep – readr would add 4 MB to the download
                                na.strings = "NA")
.dag_elsewhere <- c(
  "This page holds the adjustment sets that dagitty gives for the graph of the cell",
  "with any of its commented arrows switched on. For another graph or another",
  "question, use the downloadable workspace, where R/dag_starter.R builds the graph",
  "and dagitty answers whatever you ask of it.")

# A graph from one formula per arrow. coords is accepted, as ggdag::dagify()
# accepts it, and not used, because this page does not draw the graph. The
# arrows, sorted, are the key under which data/dag_answers.csv holds the
# answers for the graph.
dagify <- function(..., exposure = NULL, outcome = NULL, coords = NULL) {
  e <- purrr::map(list(...), \(f) {
    child <- all.vars(f[[2]])
    parent <- all.vars(f[[3]])
    data.frame(from = parent, to = rep(child, length(parent)))
  }) |>
    purrr::list_rbind()
  structure(list(edges = e, exposure = exposure, outcome = outcome,
                 nodes = unique(c(e$from, e$to)),
                 key = paste(sort(unique(paste(e$from, "->", e$to)), method = "radix"),
                             collapse = "; ")),
            class = "simple_dag")
}

# The minimal adjustment sets for the total effect of the exposure on the
# outcome, as dagitty::adjustmentSets() returns them, read from the table
adjustmentSets <- function(x, exposure = x$exposure, outcome = x$outcome, effect = "total", ...) {
  rows <- .dag_answers[.dag_answers$arrows %in% x$key &
                         .dag_answers$exposure %in% paste(exposure, collapse = ", ") &
                         .dag_answers$outcome %in% paste(outcome, collapse = ", ") &
                         .dag_answers$effect %in% effect, ]
  if (nrow(rows) == 0) {
    writeLines(.dag_elsewhere)
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  structure(strsplit(rows$answer[rows$item > 0], ", ", fixed = TRUE), class = "simple_dag_sets")
}

print.simple_dag_sets <- function(x, ...) {
  if (!length(x)) {
    writeLines("(no set of these variables closes every backdoor path)")
  } else {
    purrr::map_chr(x, \(z) if (length(z)) paste0("{ ", paste(z, collapse = ", "), " }") else "{}") |>
      writeLines()
  }
  invisible(x)
}

# Registered rather than left in the session: these cells do not evaluate in
# the global environment, so plain S3 dispatch would not find the method.
registerS3method("print", "simple_dag_sets", print.simple_dag_sets)
```

Now specify the graph. The five committed arrows are live; the arguable ones are commented out, one substantive claim per line. Uncomment any you believe, then run the cell, which stores the graph as `my_dag`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_dag <- dagify( # r-style: keep – the dagify() of this page; the workspace calls ggdag::dagify()
  # The path of interest, and the two common causes (country and year)
  # that two-way fixed effects absorb.
  framing      ~ unemployment,
  framing      ~ country,
  unemployment ~ country,
  framing      ~ year,
  unemployment ~ year,

  # GROWTH as a time-varying confounder: a slump raises unemployment and may
  # sour EU sentiment in the same year.
  # framing      ~ growth,
  # unemployment ~ growth,

  # BAILOUT as a mediator: unemployment triggers a financial-assistance
  # programme, which then shapes framing.
  # bailout ~ unemployment,
  # framing ~ bailout,

  # POLITICISATION of the EU by parties and elites as another cause of
  # framing. Multi100 instructed analysts to disregard it.
  # framing ~ politicisation,

  exposure = "unemployment",
  outcome  = "framing",
  # Coordinates for all seven nodes; the three not currently wired up are
  # simply ignored, so this block never needs editing.
  coords = list(
    x = c(unemployment = 0, framing = 3, country = 1, year = 2,
          growth = 0.9, bailout = 1.5, politicisation = 3),
    y = c(unemployment = 0, framing = 0, country = 1.4, year = 1.4,
          growth = -1.0, bailout = -1.2, politicisation = -0.95)))
```

Then ask for the adjustment set of the graph that you have just written.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
adjustmentSets(my_dag) # r-style: keep – the function of this page, which reads the answers of dagitty
```

With the five committed arrows the minimal adjustment set is `{ country, year }`, which is what a two-way fixed-effects model absorbs. An adjustment set is a set of variables that, once adjusted for, blocks every non-causal path from unemployment to framing, and it is minimal when no variable can be dropped from it without reopening one of those paths. The two-way fixed-effects model of analyst C6HJR, one of the three that you can reproduce in Task 3, therefore makes the same identification claim as the graph you have just written, while the model of KQXUE adjusts for the country alone and the random intercepts of 018OL adjust for neither in this sense.

Now uncomment the growth pair and run the two cells again. The set becomes `{ country, growth, year }`, because a slump varies within a country over time and fixed effects remove only country-constant and year-common variation, so a specification that matches your beliefs would need `growth` as a co-predictor, a choice that the adjustment-set decision of the menu offers in Task 5. The bailout arrows behave differently: a mediator lies on the path you are trying to measure, so the adjustment set does not grow when you add one, and adjusting for it would remove part of the effect that you are trying to estimate.

Write two sentences for your own notes. What do two-way fixed effects adjust for, and what can they **not** fix? (Hint: anything time-varying within a country that you have not measured.)


## Task 3 – Reproduce a recorded result {#task-3-reproduction}

This is the **reproducibility** check. Five analysts reanalysed the claim for Multi100, each with code of their own. Three of them fitted their models on aggregate data, and their recorded results reproduce exactly on this page; choose one of the three. The short session offers the first two, C6HJR and KQXUE, and the one-day workshop and the Extended course the third as well, 018OL, whose packages for mixed models download about 32 MB on the first run of its cell, which is why a participant of the short session is not sent to it. The other two, KEVF1 and PRL47, fitted theirs on several hundred thousand respondents, whose files GESIS does not allow the course to publish. Their analyses lie outside the one-day workshop; the third day of the Extended course works on the respondents, from a file that each participant builds from their own GESIS downloads.

| Analyst | Data on this page | Model | Recorded by Multi100 |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| [C6HJR](#task-3-c6hjr) | `EUframes_cy.csv`, 270 country-years | two-way fixed effects (country and year), conventional standard errors | t = −3.804 on 233 df |
| [KQXUE](#task-3-kqxue) | `analyst_KQXUE.csv`, 270 country-years | country fixed effects, conventional standard errors | t = −7.169 on 242 df |
| [018OL](#task-3-018ol) | `analyst_018OL.csv`, 420 cells of country, year and wave | random intercepts for country, year and wave, Satterthwaite degrees of freedom | t = −1.206 on 396.9 df |

Each analyst has a short run of cells below, one step to a cell, and the cells with blanks (`______`) are exercises: replace the blanks with the missing code, then press "Run Code". A hint and the full solution sit under every exercise, and using the hints and the solutions is not cheating. Run the cells of your analyst in order, because each step uses what the step before it made. When you have your value, type the analyst and the value into the chat, for example `KQXUE t = -7.169`, hold it, and send it on the facilitator's word. The two files of KQXUE and 018OL were rebuilt by the course from the GESIS waves, following the code that each analyst deposited on the OSF step by step, slips included; their [codebook](data/analyst_panels_codebook.md) says how.

### C6HJR – two-way fixed effects {#task-3-c6hjr}

Analyst C6HJR averaged the respondents of each country-year into the course panel and fitted the cosmopolitan scale on unemployment centred on its grand mean, with fixed effects for country and year:

```
mcosmo ~ unemp_c   with fixed effects for country and year
```

Multi100 recorded **t = −3.804** (df = 233, N = 270).

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: reproduce
euframes <- utils::read.csv("data/EUframes_cy.csv") # r-style: keep – readr would add 4 MB to the download
```

The first step centres the unemployment rate on its grand mean. The cell prints nothing, since it only adds the column `unemp_c` to `euframes`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: reproduce
#| envir: global
euframes <- datawizard::data_modify(euframes, unemp_c = unemp - ______)
```

:::: {.hint exercise="reproduce"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint – centring

To centre a variable on its grand mean, subtract the mean of the whole column:

``` r
euframes <- datawizard::data_modify(euframes, unemp_c = unemp - mean(unemp))
```

With fixed effects present this does not change the t-statistic, but the specification recorded for C6HJR includes it, so do it explicitly.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="reproduce"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
euframes <- datawizard::data_modify(euframes, unemp_c = unemp - mean(unemp))
```
:::
::::

The second step fits two-way fixed effects with `fixest::feols()` on the centred rate and prints the estimate.

```{webr}
#| exercise: reproduce-fe
#| envir: global
# the part after the | adds the fixed effects
m1 <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp_c | ______, data = euframes, vcov = "iid")

# digits = 5 prints enough decimals to compare t with the value on record
print(parameters::model_parameters(m1), digits = 5)
```

:::: {.hint exercise="reproduce-fe"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint – the fixed-effects syntax

In `fixest::feols`, the bar `|` separates the regression from the fixed effects. To add country and year fixed effects, list them after the bar separated by `+`:

``` r
fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp_c | cntry + year, data = euframes, vcov = "iid")
```
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="reproduce-fe"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Fully worked solution

``` r
m1 <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp_c | cntry + year, data = euframes, vcov = "iid")
# digits = 5 prints enough decimals to compare t with the value on record
print(parameters::model_parameters(m1), digits = 5)
```

You should get a coefficient of −0.00347, a standard error of 0.00091 and t(233) = −3.80372, which is the −3.804 on record to the third decimal: the recorded value reproduces from the published data and the published model. `parameters::model_parameters()` reports the estimate, its standard error, its confidence interval, the t with its degrees of freedom and the p-value of any model in one table. The argument `vcov = "iid"` asks for conventional standard errors, the kind that `plm` reported for the recorded value, which is why the two match to three decimals. Conventional errors treat the 270 country-years as independent; the case study and Part 4 show what changes when they do not.
:::
::::

### KQXUE – country fixed effects {#task-3-kqxue}

Analyst KQXUE built a country-year panel of its own in Stata. Its outcome, `cosmo`, is the cosmopolitan share of each respondent's mentions averaged over the country-year, leaving out the respondents who mention nothing, and its predictor, `unemp`, is unemployment as a percentage of the whole population aged 20–64 rather than of the labour force. The model, `xtreg cosmo unemployment, fe` in Stata, has a fixed effect for each country and none for the year, with conventional standard errors. Multi100 recorded **t = −7.169** (df = 242, N = 270).

Run this cell first. It loads the panel of KQXUE as `kqxue`, one row per country-year, and lists its columns.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
kqxue <- utils::read.csv("data/analyst_KQXUE.csv") # r-style: keep – readr would add 4 MB to the download
datawizard::data_peek(kqxue)
```

Then fit the model of KQXUE and print the estimate.

```{webr}
#| exercise: reproduce-kqxue
#| envir: global
# country fixed effects only, as xtreg ..., fe fits them in Stata
m2 <- fixest::feols(cosmo ~ unemp | ______, data = kqxue, vcov = "iid")

# digits = 5 prints enough decimals to compare t with the value on record
print(parameters::model_parameters(m2), digits = 5)
```

:::: {.hint exercise="reproduce-kqxue"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint – one set of fixed effects

`xtreg, fe` removes the average of each country and nothing else, so the bar is followed by the country alone: `| cntry`.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="reproduce-kqxue"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Fully worked solution

``` r
m2 <- fixest::feols(cosmo ~ unemp | cntry, data = kqxue, vcov = "iid")
# digits = 5 prints enough decimals to compare t with the value on record
print(parameters::model_parameters(m2), digits = 5)
```

You should get a coefficient of −0.00736, a standard error of 0.00103 and t(242) = −7.16867, the −7.169 on record. The 242 degrees of freedom are the 270 country-years less the 27 country effects and the slope. The Stata code of KQXUE appended the wave EB 62.0 twice, so the respondents of autumn 2004 count twice in the 2004 means of the fifteen older member states. The column `cosmo_once` holds the means with that wave counted once; replace `cosmo` with `cosmo_once` and run the cell again to see how little the slip moves the result.
:::
::::

### 018OL – random intercepts {#task-3-018ol}

Analyst 018OL averaged its outcome, `pos`, the mean of the five cosmopolitan items of each respondent, in cells of country, year and wave, and fitted it on the unemployment rate of those aged 15–74 with a linear mixed model that has random intercepts for country, year and wave. The analyst rescaled the outcome to run from 0 to 1 before fitting, which changes the coefficient but neither t nor its degrees of freedom. Multi100 recorded **t = −1.206** (df = 396.9, N = 420).

Run the first two cells below before the model. The first loads the file of 018OL as `o18ol`, one row per cell of country, year and wave.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
o18ol <- utils::read.csv("data/analyst_018OL.csv") # r-style: keep – readr would add 4 MB to the download
```

The model needs two packages that the page does not load at the start, `lme4` and `lmerTest`, so the second cell downloads them into your browser, about 32 MB, which can take a minute on a slow connection. Later runs start at once.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
if (!requireNamespace("lmerTest", quietly = TRUE)) webr::install(c("lme4", "lmerTest"), quiet = TRUE)
```

The next step rescales the cell means to run from 0 to 1, as the analyst did.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
o18ol <- datawizard::data_modify(o18ol, pos01 = datawizard::rescale(pos, to = c(0, 1)))
```

Then fit the model of 018OL and print its fixed effects.

```{webr}
#| exercise: reproduce-018ol
#| envir: global
# random intercepts for country, year and wave; lmerTest adds the
# Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
m3 <- lmerTest::lmer(pos01 ~ unemp + (1 | cntry) + (1 | ______) + (1 | wave), data = o18ol)

print(parameters::model_parameters(m3, effects = "fixed", ci_method = "______"), digits = 5)
```

:::: {.hint exercise="reproduce-018ol"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint – the random intercepts and the degrees of freedom

Each `(1 | x)` gives the cells that share a value of `x` an intercept of their own, so the missing one is `(1 | year)`. `parameters::model_parameters()` reports the degrees of freedom that `ci_method` names, and `lmerTest` provides the Satterthwaite approximation, `ci_method = "satterthwaite"`.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="reproduce-018ol"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Fully worked solution

``` r
m3 <- lmerTest::lmer(pos01 ~ unemp + (1 | cntry) + (1 | year) + (1 | wave), data = o18ol)
print(parameters::model_parameters(m3, effects = "fixed", ci_method = "satterthwaite"), digits = 5)
```

You should get a coefficient of −0.00203, a standard error of 0.00169 and t = −1.20627 on 396.92 degrees of freedom, the −1.206 on record. The year in the file is the one that 018OL took from the names of its data files, which put the wave EB 79.3, fielded in 2013, in 2012; the column `year_fieldwork` holds the true year. A rebuild that dates every wave by its fieldwork, and so merges the unemployment of 2013 onto those cells, gives t = −1.606 instead, so a rebuild that dates the waves correctly does not recover the recorded value.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reproduction and the five analysts

You reproduced the recorded value, and so did everyone else in the class who chose the same analyst, because each of you ran the same code on the same file. Once the data and the code are in hand, this is why reproducibility is the cheapest of the three Rs to establish; for KQXUE and 018OL, putting the data in hand meant rebuilding their files from the code that they deposited.
:::

## Task 4 – Work the menu {#task-4-explore}

This task is **exploratory**. You try several specifications, look at what each one does, and get a feel for which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. Nothing in this task is preregistered; the preregistration comes in Task 5.

`try_spec()` takes one argument per decision of the [specification menu](menu.qmd), and every argument defaults to the reproduced specification, the model of analyst C6HJR from Task 3, on which the menu and the curve are built. So changing one thing means changing one argument, and everything you do not name stays as it was in that model. Each result is one of the 864 specifications on the curve of the claim, which the page loaded with the data, so it prints at once.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Nothing changed – this is the reproduced specification, the model of C6HJR in Task 3.
try_spec()
```

The printout gives the slope `b` with its conventional standard error and *t*, the claim-aligned partial *r*, the p-value of the test that classes every point on the curve, the class of the result and its placement among the 864. The test clusters the standard errors by country with the CR2 correction and judges the *t* against Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, which count how many countries effectively carry the information, `r sprintf("%.1f", ref$df_cr2)` for the reproduced specification rather than the 27 countries of the panel, as the [module on panel data](../../companion/panel-data.qmd#sec-inference) explains; the specification lies below zero, but with a CR2 p of `r sprintf("%.4f", ref$p_cr2)` it is not significant at 5%, and `r round(100 * mean(curve$r_ca < ref$r_ca))`% of the 864 specifications lie further in the direction of the claim.

Each of the six cells below changes a single decision. The first four change the question that is being asked of the data; the last two keep the question and change only how it is measured. Run them in turn and compare the results.

The first changes the outcome from the cosmopolitan scale to the composite of both positive framings.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(outcome = "mpos")  # the composite of both positive framings
```

The second keeps the country effects and drops the year effects.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(estimator = "fe_country")  # country effects only: changes common to all of Europe stay in
```

The third measures the economy by GDP growth instead of unemployment.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(predictor = "growth")  # GDP growth instead of unemployment, in the World Bank series
```

The fourth holds GDP growth fixed, the other economic measure beside unemployment.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(copredictor = "other")  # adjusted for the other economic measure, here GDP growth
```

The fifth leaves out the respondents who mentioned no frame, instead of scoring them zero.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(noop = "drop")  # leave out the respondents who mentioned no frame
```

The sixth replaces the World Bank series of unemployment with a Eurostat series, the unemployed as a share of the whole population aged 20–64.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(measure = "es_2064_pop")  # a Eurostat unemployment series instead of the World Bank one
```

The menu holds more options than the curve, which keeps only the options that answer this claim in a justifiable way. Every other option is still an argument of `try_spec()`, so trying one is part of the exercise. The helper refuses it, gives the reason why it is not on the curve and names the page of the course that teaches it, and the [decision map](map.qmd) sets out every decision and its options on one page. Run the cell, then edit it to try others, such as `sample = "no_bailout"`, `weights = "pop"`, `construction = "count"`, `family = "beta"` or `outcome = "mneg"`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# An option that is not on the curve: the helper refuses it and says why.
try_spec(estimator = "pooled_cl")
```

Then try your own combinations. The full set of arguments, each with the reproduced specification as its default and the options of the menu in the comment beside it:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(
  # The question
  outcome      = "mcosmo",       # mcosmo | mutil | mpos          off the curve: mcomm | mlib | mneg
  predictor    = "unemp",        # unemp | growth
  copredictor  = "none",         # none | other   (the other economic measure, adjusted for)
  estimator    = "fe_twoway",    # fe_twoway | fe_country         off the curve: re | pooled_cl
  sample       = "all",          # all       off the curve: y2004_2008 | y2009_2013 | no_bailout | no_GR_ES
  weights      = "none",         # none      off the curve: n_cell | n_eff | pop
  construction = "share",        # share     off the curve: count | rate
  # Measurement
  noop         = "zero",         # zero | drop                    off the curve: split | mi_mice | mi_amelia
  item_set     = "all",          # all | un   (with or without the "unemployment" item)
  cell_weight  = "unweighted",   # unweighted | design
  measure      = "wb_nat",       # unemp:  wb_nat | es_1574_act | es_2064_pop | es_2564_lfs   off: es_1574_tips
                                 # growth: wb_growth                                          off: es_growth
  # The model
  pred_form    = "raw",          # raw | log   (growth: raw only)
  family       = "gaussian",     # gaussian  off the curve: beta
  se           = "cr2"           # cr2, fixed: CR2 errors clustered by country test every result
)
```

Everything you try is logged. Print the log to see the small multiverse that you have just built. It shows only the decisions that you varied, so the differences are easy to read:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_experiments()
```

When you have tried three or four, decide which one you would defend if you had to, run it once more so it is the most recent, and submit it. It appears on the live [Multiverse]({{< var live-results-url >}}) chart as an **exploratory** result, placed by its claim-aligned partial *r* and classed by the same CR2 test that the printout reports, and marked with the tag that the cell prints, such as `amber-otter-42`. The tag is how you find your own marks on the chart, and your declared result in Task 5 carries the same one. To choose your own, write `submit_exploration(nickname = "...")` with a nickname rather than your name, because the chart is public:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
submit_exploration()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why 'exploratory'?

Because you chose this specification after seeing what several specifications do, it lacks the guarantee that comes with a choice declared in a preregistration before its result is known – no one can rule out that it might have been chosen *because* of its result. In this course exploration is a natural step, and you also practise preregistering the analysis that you choose, so you submit twice, once here and once in Task 5.
:::

## Task 5 – Preregistration {#task-5-my-preregistration}

Preregistration means setting out your choice in a plan **before** you see what it does, which stops you from quietly picking the specification that happens to give the answer you wanted. On this page the plan is the preregistration cell below, and it binds mechanically as well: the session remembers the choices that you declare in that cell, and every later cell reads them from there. The model builder refuses code that departs from them.

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## A shortened preregistration

*Each numbered comment maps to a question in the OSF "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org" (the eight-question short form). Because you are reanalysing data that already exist, field 2 also stands in for the prior-knowledge section of the secondary-data template (van den Akker et al. 2021) – the part that AsPredicted leaves out.*
:::

Make one choice on each decision of the [specification menu](menu.qmd), complete the dotted lines, then run the cell. The menu has fourteen decisions in three groups. The seven decisions about the question fix what you are asking, the four measurement decisions fix how that question is measured, and the three decisions about the model fix how it is estimated. The curve of 864 specifications keeps two or more options on nine of these decisions and a single option on the other five, which are the sample, the weighting, the scoring rule, the model family and the inference. An option that is not on the curve stops `prereg()` with the reason why, as it stops `try_spec()`. `claim_align <- TRUE` is the course convention, applied automatically: the claim expects framing to rise with GDP growth, so the sign of a growth slope is flipped, and 'supports the claim' reads as a negative sign for everyone.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# ============================================================================
# MY PREREGISTRATION – one specification, declared before seeing its result
# ============================================================================
# 1. The claim I am testing: .................................................
# 2. The data + what I already know: EUframes_cy.csv (270 country-years,
#    public); I know that the reproduced specification gives t = -3.804,
#    and what my exploration in Task 4 showed.
# 3. My one specification – one choice on each decision. An option that is
#    not on the curve of 864 stops prereg() with the reason why.

# The question (each of these changes what is being estimated)
my_outcome      <- "mcosmo"       # mcosmo | mutil | mpos   (the positive framings)
my_predictor    <- "unemp"        # unemp | growth    (the measure whose coefficient tests the claim)
my_copredictor  <- "none"         # none | other      (the other economic measure, adjusted for)
my_estimator    <- "fe_twoway"    # fe_twoway | fe_country
my_sample       <- "all"          # all    (the 27 member states, 2004–2013)
my_weights      <- "none"         # none   (every country-year counts once)
my_construction <- "share"        # share  (the share of a respondent's own mentions)

# Measurement (the same question, put to the data differently)
my_noop         <- "zero"         # zero | drop   (respondents who mentioned no frame at all)
my_item_set     <- "all"          # all | un   (with or without the "unemployment" item)
my_cell_weight  <- "unweighted"   # unweighted | design   (cells as interviewed, or weighted)
my_measure      <- "wb_nat"       # unemp:  wb_nat | es_1574_act | es_2064_pop | es_2564_lfs
                                  # growth: wb_growth

# The model (the same question and measures, another fit)
my_pred_form    <- "raw"          # raw | log   (growth: raw only; centring or z-scaling
                                  #              would leave t, r and p unchanged)
my_family       <- "gaussian"     # gaussian   (a linear model of the cell means)
my_se           <- "cr2"          # cr2   (fixed: CR2 errors clustered by country)

claim_align     <- TRUE           # the course convention, applied automatically

# 4. Why these controls, in one DAG-grounded sentence: .......................
# 5. Supported if the claim-aligned coefficient is negative with CR2
#    p < .05; undermined if it is not significant or positive. I will
#    report what I get.
```

Then run `prereg()`, which checks every choice against the menu and prints your preregistration.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
prereg()
```

An optional mirror form collects preregistrations from the class, and its link is shared in the session. It is not required. The preregistration cell, copied into your notes, is your preregistration record.



## Task 5, continued – build, run and report {#task-5-build-run-report}

This is the **robustness** check, and it is the part that your classmates cannot copy from you: together the class samples the multiverse of defensible analyses. You have declared your specification. Now translate it into model syntax yourself, filling the three gaps – the outcome, the right-hand side, and the estimator code – as you preregistered them. `build_model()` reads your declaration and accepts nothing else, and its error messages tell you what is off. Write the log form as `log(unemp)`, and add any co-predictor with `+`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_model <- build_model(______ ~ ______, estimator = "______")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint – from menu speak to model syntax

The formula uses the column names of `euframes`, with the outcome that you preregistered on the left of `~` and the predictor terms on the right. For a declaration of the reproduced specification it is `mcosmo ~ unemp`. With the log form it would be `mcosmo ~ log(unemp)`, and with a co-predictor `mcosmo ~ unemp + growth`. The estimator is the menu code itself, in quotes: `"fe_twoway"` or `"fe_country"`. You do not write the fixed-effects syntax here – the estimator code stands for it, and the cells of C6HJR and KQXUE in Task 3 showed what it expands to. Apart from the log form, the measurement decisions and the decisions about the model never appear in the formula. They select which version of the panel the result was computed on.
:::

When the model is accepted, run it. Every specification on the curve is pre-computed: the page loaded the results of all 864 with the data, and `run_spec()` picks the one that matches your declaration. These are the numbers that the downloadable workspace gives when it fits the model and computes its CR2 test on your own machine, and here you get them without downloading the estimation packages into your browser:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
run_spec(my_model)
```

The output has the same lines as in Task 4, and the placement is the share of the 864 specifications on the curve that lie further in the direction of the claim than yours, `r round(100 * mean(curve$r_ca < ref$r_ca))`% for the reproduced specification, the model of C6HJR in Task 3.

Now send it to the class chart. The submission is built from your declaration, so there is nothing to fill in or transcribe. The cell prints your submission line and a pre-filled form link; click it and press **Send**. Your dot joins the live [Multiverse]({{< var live-results-url >}}) chart within seconds, this time labelled **declared** and carrying the same tag as your exploratory result. If you have reloaded this page since Task 4, the session has forgotten that tag, so pass it back with `report_result(nickname = "your-tag")`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
report_result()
```

If the form will not open on your machine, read the printed numbers to the facilitator, who adds your dot to the chart.

If you want a second declared specification, edit the preregistration cell, rerun `prereg()`, rebuild and rerun. The chart will still label it declared, so be clear with yourself about what the second one is. Your first declaration was made without knowing its result. Anything after it was not, which puts it back in the same category as Task 4, and you should say so wherever you write about the result.

Putting that work under version control and publishing the rendered report is the natural next step.
